| EDA | Design software, emulation hardware | Multi-year licences, largely recurring | Very high (often 80%+) | Very low |
| Semiconductor IP | Cores and interfaces | Upfront licence fee + royalty per chip shipped | Very high (often 80%+) | Very low |
| Fabless | Chips | Units x average selling price (ASP); design wins drive future revenue | High (often 50-70%) | Low |
| Foundry | Processed wafers | Price per wafer, by technology node | Wide range (about 20-60%), set by node leadership and utilisation | Very high |
| IDM | Its own chips (analogue, power, microcontrollers, memory) | Units x ASP | Roughly 40-65%; memory swings from below zero to above 50% | Medium to high |
| OSAT | Packaging and test services | Price per unit or per wafer | Low (roughly 15-25%) | Medium to high |
| Equipment | Tools for fabs, plus services | System sales + recurring services on the installed base | Roughly 40-50%, higher for leaders | Low |
| Materials | Wafers, chemicals, gases, masks | Volume x price, often under long-term agreements | Roughly 25-45% | Medium |

The ranges are indicative through-cycle levels for established players; leaders and laggards differ widely. The logic is durable: **margins follow scarcity and IP**. Software and IP sit at the top; services that customers can source elsewhere (packaging, test, trailing-edge wafers) sit lower.

R&D is the other big cost line: fabless, EDA and IP companies typically spend between a fifth and a third of revenue on it.

sections.h: Capital intensity and operating leverage
sections.body:
A fab is a **fixed-cost machine**: most of its cost is depreciation of very expensive equipment, plus facilities and staff. Revenue depends on how full it is, so **utilisation drives gross margin**.

**Gross profit = wafers x (price - variable cost per wafer) - fixed costs**

Consequences:
- A small fall in volume causes a large fall in profit (in the worked example, revenue -22% and gross profit -58%).
- In downturns IDMs and foundries report **underutilisation charges** and cut capex; in upturns margins expand quickly.
- Each new leading-edge node costs more to develop and needs a more expensive fab, which concentrates the leading edge in very few hands.

**Fabless versus foundry**: the fabless company pays for capacity through the wafer price, so its gross margin is high, but its big costs (R&D and SG&A) sit below gross profit. The foundry's depreciation sits inside COGS, so its gross margin is lower, but its EBITDA margin can be higher because depreciation is added back. That is why **EV/EBITDA flatters capital-intensive businesses**: compare them on EV/EBIT, EV/(EBITDA - capex) or FCF yield.

sections.h: The KPIs analysts track
sections.body:
| Business | KPIs |
|---|---|
| EDA and IP | Share of recurring revenue, backlog or remaining performance obligations, renewal rates, royalty revenue (units x royalty per unit), new licences |
| Fabless | Revenue by end market, gross margin, R&D / revenue, design wins, units and ASP, inventory days (own and in the channel), customer concentration |
| Foundry | Utilisation, wafer shipments (12-inch equivalent), revenue per wafer, revenue by node, capex / revenue, capacity (wafer starts per month) |
| IDM | Utilisation, inventory days, gross margin and underutilisation charges; for memory, bit growth, price per bit and cost per bit |
| OSAT | Utilisation, share of advanced packaging, capex / revenue |
| Equipment | Orders, **book-to-bill**, backlog, services share of revenue, customer concentration |
| Materials | Volumes linked to wafer starts, contract pricing, share of revenue under long-term agreements |

Three formulas that work across the chain:
- **Book-to-bill = orders / revenue**: above 1 means the backlog is building.
- **Inventory days = inventory / COGS x 365**: rising days with falling sales announce a correction and possible write-downs.
- **Capex / revenue**: the capital intensity of the model; for chipmakers, it is also next year's demand for equipment.

sections.h: Cyclicality: why semis swing more than their end markets
sections.body:
End demand (phones, cars, servers) moves by a few per cent; chip and equipment revenue can move by tens of per cent. Four amplifiers:

1. **Inventory (the bullwhip effect)**: if end demand falls 5% and customers also cut their inventory from 12 to 9 weeks of supply, their chip orders in that quarter fall by about 30%.
2. **Lead times and double ordering**: in shortages customers over-order to secure supply; when lead times normalise, orders collapse.
3. **Lumpy capacity**: fabs take years to build and come in large steps, so new supply often arrives when demand has already turned.
4. **Capex depends on the change in demand**: equipment orders follow capacity **additions**, so a slowdown in chip growth can cut equipment demand sharply (see the worked example).

**Memory** is the most cyclical segment: products are close to commodities and the price per bit swings with the balance of supply and demand.

Leading indicators: book-to-bill, inventory days (at companies and in the channel), lead times, utilisation and customers' capex plans. Long-term growth comes from rising **semiconductor content** per device (cars, data centres, industrial automation), so the cycle moves around a rising trend.

sections.h: Questions interviewers ask about semis
sections.body:
- **'Why does a fabless company have a higher gross margin than a foundry, but often a lower EBITDA margin?'** Its COGS is wafers bought at a price that already includes the foundry's margin and depreciation, while its big costs, R&D and SG&A, sit below gross profit. The foundry's depreciation is in COGS and is added back in EBITDA.
- **'Why is equipment more cyclical than chips?'** Equipment demand depends on capacity additions, i.e. on the change in chip demand, not on its level.
- **'What happens to a foundry when utilisation falls from 90% to 70%?'** Revenue falls in proportion, fixed costs stay, and the gross margin collapses.
- **'What is Moore's law and why does it matter economically?'** Transistor density has historically doubled roughly every two years, lowering the cost per transistor; but each new node costs more to design and to build, which rewards scale and pushes alternatives such as advanced packaging.
- **'What is a design win?'** A customer selects your chip for its product. Revenue follows when the product ramps, often a year or more later, and lasts for the product's life, many years in automotive and industrial. It gives visibility and creates switching costs.

sections.h: How to say it in an interview
sections.body:
- 'The chain runs from EDA and IP, through design by fabless companies and IDMs, to manufacturing at foundries or IDM fabs using equipment and materials, and then packaging and test. Margins follow scarcity and IP: EDA and IP at the top, packaging and test at the bottom.'
- 'A fab is a fixed-cost business, so utilisation drives margins; that is why I'd compare a foundry with a fabless peer on EV/EBIT or EBITDA minus capex rather than on EV/EBITDA.'
- 'Equipment is the most cyclical part of the chain because it depends on the change in chip demand, so I watch book-to-bill, inventory days and customers' capex plans.'

examples.q: A fab has a capacity of 100,000 wafers a year, sells at 6,000 per wafer, has fixed costs of 250m a year and variable costs of 1,500 per wafer. What are revenue, gross profit and gross margin at 90% and at 70% utilisation, and what is the break-even utilisation?
steps: 90%: 90,000 wafers; revenue 540m; variable costs 135m; gross profit 540 - 135 - 250 = 155m; gross margin 28.7%.
70%: 70,000 wafers; revenue 420m; variable costs 105m; gross profit 420 - 105 - 250 = 65m; gross margin 15.5%.
Revenue -22.2%, gross profit -58.1%: operating leverage of about 2.6x.
examples.answer: Gross profit 155m (28.7% margin) at 90% and 65m (15.5%) at 70%; break-even at about 56% utilisation.

examples.q: Fabless company: revenue 1,000, EBITDA 330, capex 30, D&A 30. Foundry: revenue 1,000, EBITDA 500, capex 350, D&A 250. Both trade at 10.0x EV/EBITDA. Compare them on EV/EBIT and on EV/(EBITDA - capex).
steps: EBIT: fabless 330 - 30 = 300; foundry 500 - 250 = 250. EV/EBIT: 11.0x versus 20.0x.
EBITDA - capex: fabless 300 (91% of EBITDA); foundry 150 (30%). EV/(EBITDA - capex): 11.0x versus 33.3x.

Same EV/EBITDA, very different prices for the cash each business generates: the foundry is far more expensive per euro of cash, and only growth (capex above D&A builds future capacity) can justify it.
examples.answer: Fabless 11.0x on both measures; foundry 20.0x EV/EBIT and 33.3x EV/(EBITDA - capex).

examples.q: Chipmakers' capex = 50 of maintenance + 10 per unit of new capacity. Capacity is 100 and tracks demand. Demand grows 20% in year 1, 5% in year 2 and 10% in year 3. What happens to equipment demand (capex)?
steps: Year 1: capacity added = 20% x 100 = 20; capex = 50 + 200 = 250. Capacity becomes 120.
Year 2: added = 5% x 120 = 6; capex = 50 + 60 = 110, a fall of 56% while chip demand is still growing.
Year 3: added = 10% x 126 = 12.6; capex = 50 + 126 = 176, a rise of 60%.
Equipment revenue follows the change in chip growth, not its level: the accelerator effect.
examples.answer: Capex goes 250, 110, 176: -56% and then +60%, while chip demand grows every year.

examples.q: A fabless company had inventory of 300 and annual COGS of 1,320 a year ago; today inventory is 450 and annualised COGS is 1,200. Calculate inventory days and say what they signal.
steps: A year ago: 300 / 1,320 x 365 = 83 days.
Inventory is up 50% while COGS is down 9%: the company is building stock faster than it sells.
Signal: a correction is likely (lower wafer orders to the foundry, price pressure), with a risk of inventory write-downs and gross margin pressure in the coming quarters; check channel inventory too.
examples.answer: Inventory days rise from about 83 to about 137: an early warning of a downturn and of possible write-downs.

cheatsheet: Chain: EDA and IP -> design (fabless, IDM) -> fab (foundry, IDM) with equipment and materials -> packaging and test -> systems.
Margins follow scarcity and IP: EDA and IP highest, OSAT lowest.
Fabless: asset-light, R&D-heavy. Foundry and IDM: capex-heavy, utilisation-driven.
Fab gross profit = wafers x (price - variable cost) - fixed costs.
Capital-intensive versus asset-light: compare on EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA - capex), not EV/EBITDA.
Book-to-bill = orders / revenue; inventory days = inventory / COGS x 365.
Equipment demand depends on the change in chip demand: the accelerator effect.
Memory is the most cyclical segment: the price per bit follows supply and demand.
Moore's law: cost per transistor falls, but each node costs more to design and to build.

lessons.title: How tech and semiconductor deals are valued and why they happen
lessons.summary: You will be able to choose the right multiple for each tech business, read SaaS KPIs, explain the strategic logic and synergies of tech and chip deals, flag the regulatory risks, value pre-revenue deep tech and pitch a recent deal in two minutes.

sections.h: Which multiple for which tech business
sections.body:
| Business | Main multiples | Why |
|---|---|---|
| SaaS and software | EV/NTM revenue, EV/ARR; EV/FCF and P/E once mature | Growth spending depresses margins; recurring revenue drives value |
| EDA and semiconductor IP | EV/revenue, EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF | Recurring revenue, very high margins, almost no capex |
| Fabless | EV/EBITDA, P/E on NTM; EV/revenue for high growth | Asset-light, earnings are meaningful |
| Foundry and IDM | EV/EBITDA and EV/EBIT through the cycle; P/B at the trough | Capital-intensive: depreciation is a real cost and book value anchors in downturns |
| Memory | P/B, EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle earnings | Earnings swing too much for P/E |
| Equipment | P/E and EV/EBIT on mid-cycle earnings | Cyclical orders, low capex |
| OSAT | EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT | Capital-intensive services, lower margins |
| IT services | EV/EBITDA, P/E | People-based, stable margins |

**The cyclical paradox**: at the trough earnings are depressed, so the P/E looks high; at the peak earnings are inflated, so the P/E looks low. Value cyclicals on **normalised (mid-cycle) earnings**, and remember that chip stocks often look 'expensive' at the best time to buy.

For precedents, prefer deals done at a similar point in the cycle, and check whether the multiples are on LTM or NTM figures: for a fast-growing or recovering business the difference is large.

sections.h: SaaS KPIs that drive the multiple
sections.body:
- **ARR** (annual recurring revenue): the annualised value of subscription contracts at a date.
- **Net new ARR = new + expansion - contraction - churn.**
- **NRR (net revenue retention) = (starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / starting ARR**, measured on the customers at the start of the period. Above 100% means the business grows even without new customers.
- **GRR (gross revenue retention) = (starting ARR - contraction - churn) / starting ARR**: the quality of the base, at most 100%.
- **Gross margin**: typically 70-85% for software; hosting and services lower it.
- **CAC payback = sales and marketing spend / (new ARR x gross margin)**: how long new customers take to repay what it cost to win them.
- **LTV / CAC**: the lifetime gross profit of a customer over the cost of acquiring it; 3x or more is the usual benchmark.
- **RPO and billings**: contracted revenue not yet recognised; revenue + change in deferred revenue.
- **Rule of 40**: growth % + margin % >= 40 (see the lesson on high-growth valuation).

What moves the multiple most: growth, NRR and the path to FCF. A company with 120% NRR compounds its base; one with 85% GRR must replace 15% of its ARR every year before it can grow.

sections.h: Why tech and semiconductor deals happen
sections.body:
Five recurring rationales, often combined:
1. **Buy versus build (time to market)**: a proven design team and IP portfolio can take years to build; buying one is faster and less risky.
2. **Scale in R&D**: design costs rise with every node, so spreading them over more revenue is a lasting advantage; consolidation in mature segments (analogue, memory, equipment) also brings cost synergies.
3. **Portfolio breadth**: selling a complete solution to the same customer (processor + connectivity + power + software) and cross-selling through a larger sales force.
4. **Vertical integration**: system companies bringing chip design in house, chipmakers adding software to capture more value, or securing scarce capacity (advanced packaging, specialty processes).
5. **Talent and technology**: scarce engineering teams (AI architectures, RF, analogue, power) and patents; at the extreme, an acqui-hire.

Financial sponsors add their own logic: carve-outs of non-core divisions from large groups, take-privates of mature software companies with recurring revenue, and buy-and-build platforms in fragmented niches (test services, components, IT services).

sections.h: Synergies in tech deals
sections.body:
- **Cost**: overlapping R&D roadmaps, SG&A and back office, purchasing power with foundries and OSATs, fab consolidation for IDMs, distribution.
- **Revenue**: cross-selling to the combined customer base, bundles and higher attach rates, entry into the partner's end markets. Discount them heavily: they depend on customers' decisions.
- **Capex**: avoiding a new fab or production line by using the partner's capacity.

**Post-synergy multiple = price / (EBITDA + run-rate synergies)**: the number bankers use to defend a high headline multiple.

Tech-specific dis-synergies:
- **Talent flight**: engineers leave after closing; retention packages (often in shares) are part of the cost of the deal.
- **Customer reaction**: customers that compete with the acquirer may dual-source or switch.
- **Roadmap disruption**: cutting overlapping R&D too fast can destroy the very products the buyer paid for.

R&D cost synergies are credible only if the roadmaps really overlap; in deep tech the value usually lies in keeping the team intact, not in cutting it.

sections.h: Regulatory risks: merger control, investment screening and export controls
sections.body:
Tech and chip deals carry three generic regulatory risks that can delay, reshape or block a transaction:

- **Merger control (antitrust)**: horizontal overlaps in product markets, and vertical concerns when the combined group could **foreclose** rivals from a key input (IP, equipment, a component) or from customers. Remedies: divestments, or behavioural commitments such as continued supply and interoperability.
- **Foreign investment screening**: many jurisdictions review acquisitions by foreign investors of companies active in semiconductors and other critical technologies, sometimes including minority stakes. Outcomes: clearance, clearance with conditions (governance limits, ring-fencing of sensitive activities, supply commitments) or prohibition.
- **Export controls**: licences may be required to ship certain technologies, software or know-how to certain destinations or end users, and sharing controlled technology with foreign staff can itself count as an export. In due diligence: product classification, the customer base by destination, compliance history and any voluntary disclosures. Controls can shrink the addressable market and complicate integration.

How deals protect themselves: a realistic **long-stop date** with extensions, clear **efforts** obligations (which remedies the buyer must accept), **reverse break fees** if approvals fail, pre-agreed remedies, and sometimes carving out a sensitive business before signing.

In an interview, discuss these risks as mechanisms, not as predictions about specific governments.

sections.h: Valuing pre-revenue deep tech
sections.body:
No revenue, no earnings to compare, binary technical risk. Four methods, best used together:

1. **Risk-adjusted NPV (rNPV) by milestones**: the success value at a horizon, multiplied by the cumulative probability of passing each milestone (prototype, customer qualification, volume production), minus the expected funding costs, discounted at a rate that reflects the remaining market risk.
2. **Comparable rounds and acquisitions**: post-money valuations of companies at a similar stage; read the terms (liquidation preferences, caps) as well as the headline.
3. **Cost to recreate**: engineer-years x fully loaded cost + equipment + a premium for the time saved; often the buyer's real benchmark in a buy-versus-build decision.
4. **VC method and scenarios**: see the lesson on high-growth valuation.

Diligence questions that move value: technology readiness (lab, prototype, qualified), IP ownership and freedom to operate, the path to manufacturing (foundry access, yields), customer engagement (design-ins, letters of intent) and cash runway.

sections.h: A framework to pitch a recent tech deal
sections.body:
'Tell me about a tech deal you have followed.' Use six steps and about two minutes, with public information only:

1. **The facts in one sentence**: who buys whom, for how much (EV and multiple), paid how, expected closing.
2. **Why**: the strategic rationale, in two points (from the list above).
3. **Price**: the multiple against peers and precedents, the premium, the post-synergy multiple.
4. **Structure and financing**: cash, shares or debt; the impact on leverage, rating and EPS.
5. **Risks**: regulatory approvals, integration and talent, the cycle.
6. **Your view and what to watch**: one judgement and one indicator to follow (approval timing, synergy delivery, customer reaction).

Prepare two deals: one in semiconductors and one in software. Never use deals you have worked on unless they are public, and even then use only public facts.

sections.h: How to say it in an interview
sections.body:
- 'For software I'd look at EV to NTM revenue against growth, NRR and the rule of 40; for semis, at EV/EBIT or P/E on mid-cycle earnings, because trough earnings make cyclicals look expensive exactly when they are cheap.'
- 'The deal makes sense on a post-synergy basis: 25 times EBITDA headline, but about 17 times including run-rate cost synergies, against peers at 20 times; the risk is delivering those synergies without losing the engineers.'
- 'The key risks are regulatory, from merger control, foreign investment screening and export controls, which is why I'd expect an extended long-stop date and a reverse break fee.'

examples.q: A SaaS company starts the year with ARR of 100. During the year it adds 30 of ARR from new customers and 15 of expansion, and loses 3 to downgrades and 7 to churn. Sales and marketing spend was 36 and the gross margin is 80%. Calculate ending ARR, growth, NRR, GRR and CAC payback.
steps: Ending ARR = 100 + 30 + 15 - 3 - 7 = 135: growth of 35%.
CAC payback = 36 / (30 x 80%) = 1.5 years = 18 months.
Reading: healthy expansion, but 10% of the base is lost every year and must be replaced before the company can grow.
examples.answer: ARR 135 (+35%), NRR 105%, GRR 90%, CAC payback 18 months.

examples.q: An equipment maker earns EPS of 2.00 at the trough of the cycle, 4.00 mid-cycle and 6.00 at the peak. The market values it at 15x mid-cycle EPS. What is the fair price, and what P/E does that price show at the trough and at the peak?
steps: Fair price = 15 x 4.00 = 60.
At the trough: 60 / 2.00 = 30x, so it looks expensive.
At the peak: 60 / 6.00 = 10x, so it looks cheap.
An investor using the spot P/E would sell at the trough and buy at the peak, exactly the wrong way round: value cyclicals on normalised earnings.
examples.answer: Fair price 60: 30x trough EPS and 10x peak EPS for the same value.

examples.q: A chip-design start-up would be worth 1,000 in year 5 if it succeeds. It must pass three milestones: prototype (60% probability), customer qualification (50%) and volume production (70%). It needs 60 of funding now and 40 in year 2 if the prototype works. The discount rate is 15%. What is the risk-adjusted NPV, and what would a naive success-case DCF give?
steps: Cumulative probability of success = 0.6 x 0.5 x 0.7 = 21%.
rNPV = 104.4 - 78.1 = 26.3. A success-case DCF (1,000 / 1.15^5 - 60 - 40 / 1.15^2 = 406.9) overstates the value about 15 times.
examples.answer: An rNPV of about 26, against about 407 for the naive success case.

examples.q: A buyer offers an EV of 3,000 for a fictional analogue chip company with NTM revenue of 400 and NTM EBITDA of 120. Peers trade at 6.0x revenue and 20.0x EBITDA. The buyer announces run-rate cost synergies of 60. Build the valuation line of your pitch.
steps: Headline multiples: 3,000 / 400 = 7.5x revenue and 3,000 / 120 = 25.0x EBITDA.
Peer-implied value: 20.0 x 120 = 2,400 (and 6.0 x 400 = 2,400), so the price is a 25% premium to peers.
Post-synergy multiple: 3,000 / (120 + 60) = 16.7x, below the peers' 20.0x.
Pitch line: 'expensive on a standalone basis at 25 times EBITDA, but under 17 times after synergies, so the deal works if the buyer delivers the 60 of savings and keeps the team'.
examples.answer: 7.5x revenue and 25.0x EBITDA headline; 16.7x after synergies, against peers at 20.0x.

cheatsheet: Software: EV/NTM revenue or EV/ARR, read together with growth, NRR and the rule of 40.
Fabless and IP: EV/EBITDA and P/E. Capital-heavy fabs: EV/EBIT, EBITDA - capex, P/B at the trough.
Cyclicals: value on mid-cycle earnings; high P/E at the trough, low P/E at the peak.
NRR = (starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / starting ARR.
CAC payback = S&M spend / (new ARR x gross margin).
Deal logic: buy versus build, scale in R&D, portfolio breadth, vertical integration, talent and technology.
Post-synergy multiple = price / (EBITDA + run-rate synergies).
Regulatory risk: merger control, investment screening, export controls; protect with long-stop dates and reverse break fees.
Deep tech: rNPV = probability x discounted success value - expected discounted funding.
Deal pitch: facts, rationale, price, structure, risks, view.
